client: I just started this new marketing job a few weeks ago, and I already feel like I'm drowning. Everyone else on the team seems to know exactly what they're doing, while I'm constantly scrambling to meet deadlines and second-guessing all my work. I keep lying awake at night worrying that they'll realize they made a mistake hiring me.
therapist: It sounds like you're putting a lot of pressure on yourself to perform perfectly in this new role. I notice you're comparing yourself to others who've been there longer - what would it be like to give yourself permission to be new at this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it’s hard not to compare myself when everyone around me seems so confident and capable. I feel like I’m constantly falling short, and it’s exhausting trying to keep up. Giving myself permission to be new feels almost like letting myself off the hook, and I worry that if I do that, I’ll just fall even further behind.
therapist: The way you describe this sounds like you're holding yourself to an incredibly high standard - where did this belief come from that you can't afford to be learning? I hear the exhaustion in your voice when you talk about trying to keep up.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I guess it came from my parents always pushing me to be perfect growing up. If I got a B instead of an A, it was like I'd failed completely. Now I feel like if I'm not constantly achieving, I'm falling behind and disappointing everyone. 

But it's exhausting - I'm so tired of feeling like I can never relax or make mistakes. Even admitting that makes me feel guilty though, like I'm just making excuses.
therapist: It sounds like those early messages about perfection have really stayed with you. What would it feel like to challenge that belief that making mistakes means you're disappointing people?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, the idea of challenging that belief makes me feel kind of panicky. Like if I stop trying to be perfect, everything will fall apart and people will see how inadequate I really am. But at the same time, I'm so exhausted from constantly trying to meet impossible standards.
therapist: I hear both the fear in your voice about what might happen if you let go of perfectionism, and also the deep exhaustion from maintaining it. That tension between wanting to change but fearing the consequences must feel overwhelming at times.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, it is exhausting. I know my perfectionism is making me miserable, but I can't shake the feeling that if I lower my standards even a little, everything will fall apart. What if I become lazy or people think less of me? 

That fear keeps me stuck in this cycle, even though I'm constantly stressed and never feel good enough. It's like my brain tells me perfection is the only safe option.
therapist: You're describing this painful cycle so clearly - where perfectionism feels like both the problem and the only solution. I wonder if we could explore what "good enough" might look like for you, without it meaning you're being lazy?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: "I get what you're saying about 'good enough,' but honestly, the idea of lowering my standards makes me anxious. If I’m not striving for perfection, I feel like I’m failing or letting people down. It’s like I’m stuck between two bad options—being overwhelmed by perfectionism or feeling guilty for not doing enough."
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two difficult choices right now, where both paths feel painful in different ways. What do you think keeps perfectionism feeling like the "safer" option, even though it's causing you so much stress?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think perfectionism feels safer because at least when I fail, I can tell myself I tried my absolute best. If I lower my standards and still fail, it feels like I didn’t even deserve to succeed in the first place. But you’re right—it’s exhausting, and I feel like I’m never good enough no matter how much I do.
therapist: It sounds like perfectionism gives you a sense of control, even though it comes with such a heavy cost. I wonder if there’s a middle ground where you could still feel like you’re giving your best effort, without it needing to be "perfect"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about finding a middle ground, but the idea of not doing things perfectly makes me really anxious. What if "good enough" actually means I'm failing? I've built my whole identity around being the person who never makes mistakes.
therapist: It sounds like this fear of failure is deeply tied to how you see yourself as a person. What would it mean for you if, just once, you allowed yourself to make a small mistake without it defining your worth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... the idea of making a mistake still makes my stomach twist up. Even if it's small, I feel like it proves I'm not good enough. People might see through me and realize I'm not as competent as they think.
therapist: I hear how deeply unsettling this idea feels for you - like making even a small mistake would unravel everything. That fear seems to be holding on tight, even as it keeps you trapped in this exhausting cycle. What do you imagine would actually happen if someone noticed a small error?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I don't know exactly what would happen, but I just know it would be bad. People would probably think I'm incompetent or careless, even if it's just a tiny mistake. The worst part is I can't even explain why I feel this way - it just feels like my whole worth depends on being perfect.
therapist: It sounds like this fear of making mistakes carries so much weight for you, even if the consequences aren't clear. That sense of your worth being tied to perfection must feel like an incredible burden to carry every day. What do you think it would take to start separating "making a mistake" from "being a failure"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
